newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. Africa's Inkatha weighs constitutional role.
newsitem.headline: S. Africa's Inkatha weighs constitutional role.

text.p: South African Zulu chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi's Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP), promising not to block progress, on Wednesday sought a way back into negotiations on a final blueprint for post-apartheid rule.

"We are looking for an inclusive settlement. We're not going to come back to be obstructive," IFP strategist Walter Felgate told Reuters after two hours of talks with African National Congress (ANC) chief negotiator Cyril Ramaphosa.

He said a four-man Inkatha delegation made proposals on the timetable and substance of a possible contribution and would consult Buthelezi on a final decision whether to end the party's boycott of the constitution-writing process.

The IFP walked out of the Constitutional Assembly early last year in a row over the powers of provincial governments and was the only one of seven parties in parliament not there when the draft constitution was adopted in May.

The Constitutional Court recently returned the draft text designed to cement South Africa's 2-1/2-year-old democracy, saying inadequate powers had been allocated to provinces and that measures to protect a proposed Bill of Rights against arbitrary amendment were too weak.
Ramaphosa, who is also chairman of the Constitutional Assembly, has set October 7 as the deadline for finalisation of amendments in line with the court's 160-page judgment.
Senior IFP negotiator Ben Ngubane said after the meeting with Ramaphosa that the deadline would have to be extended if Inkatha was to play a meaningful role.
"We are worried about the scope of the discussion and also the time frames.... We want room to really address issues and not be pressured by time," he said.
Inkatha did not join negotiations that began immediately afterwards about proposals to repair the flaws in the draft constitution.

Senior ANC negotiator Mohammed Valli Moosa told Reuters that if it did return, the IFP would be free to make any proposal on any issue raised by the Constitutional Court, including the relationship with provincial governments.
"We have to reconsider provincial powers, there is no question about it. The court has ruled that the powers were substantially diminished.
"I don't see any reason why the IFP should stay out. We've accommodated them as far as the timetables are concerned...and they can make their own proposals," he said.
